title: TikTok deep cuts: animals 01 (61-75 s, Creator Rewards)
_note: TikTok Money desk 2026-10-26: deep (61-75 s) versions of queued sub-60 s animal TikToks, which earn $0 under Creator Rewards. Each: mid-action past-tense open with a frame-0 headline, 'See, in...' rewind, promise + 2 decoys + payoff at 50-70%, ironic kicker; theme 'animals'; early ask kit (guess card ~3-6 s, subscribe pill ~6-10 s, reminder before the kicker); host beats about every 15 s; one Fork. Photos are the licence-checked iNaturalist research-grade CC0/CC BY pictures of the original pack (whole animal). Facts re-checked 10/26; sources on each hook beat. Rendered one myth at a time into episodes/tt-deep-01/tt-<myth>.mp4.

beats.say: A scientist drove a car right over a tiny beetle. It got up and walked away.
beats.headline: RUN OVER. FINE.
beats.loop_say: Don't test it on me. Because
beats.short_title: This Beetle Survives Being Run Over by a Car 🪲
beats.comment: What would you make uncrushable? 🪲 phone / 🚗 car / 🍝 me
beats.bonus: The diabolical ironclad beetle's shell takes about 39,000 times its body weight; its wing cases lock together with jigsaw-like joints.
beats.caption: Beetle that survives being run over by a car: the diabolical ironclad beetle. How did it survive? 🛡️ thick shell / 🧩 something else? #beetle #animalfacts #insects #science Follow Meatball for more 🍝
sources: Rivera et al. 2020, Nature 586: 543-548, 'Toughening mechanisms of the elytra of the diabolical ironclad beetle': exoskeleton withstands ~149 N (~39,000x body weight); fused elytra joined by interlocking jigsaw-like blades that delaminate gradually instead of snapping — https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2813-8
CNN 2020-10-21: the team ran one over with a Toyota Camry and it survived; inspiration for tougher fasteners for aircraft — https://edition.cnn.com/2020/10/21/world/beetle-engineering-intl-scli-scn

Purdue University news 2020: lives under the bark of trees in western North America, eats fungus, can't fly (fused wing cases); entomologists need a drill to pin specimens — https://www.purdue.edu/newsroom/releases/2020/Q4/diabolical-ironclad-beetles-are-nearly-uncrushable.-heres-why.html

beats.say: How did it survive? Guess before I tell you.
Subscribe. I face a new animal every day.
See, in 2020, scientists in California tested the diabolical ironclad beetle.
They pressed on it until it broke. It took about 39,000 times its own weight.
That's like me holding up a cruise ship. I can't hold up a plate.
Guess one: its shell is just super thick. Nope. Thickness alone doesn't explain it.
Guess two: it hides in metal. Also no. It lives under tree bark and eats fungus.
So I lay down next to it and let them press on me. Crumbs everywhere.
Wait, here's the thing. Its wing cases are welded shut. It can't even fly.
The answer: down the middle, the two halves lock together like jigsaw puzzle pieces.
When something crushes it, the pieces peel apart slowly instead of snapping.
Bug collectors can't push a pin through it. They have to drill a hole first.
One fork, and I fall apart.
Did you guess right? Comment.
Engineers now copy its joints to build tougher airplane parts. From a beetle that eats mold under a log.
I stepped on a rock in a coral reef. Then the rock stung me.
beats.headline: THE ROCK BIT ME
beats.loop_say: So before you sit on a rock,
beats.short_title: Stonefish Are the Most Venomous Fish, and They Look Like Rocks 🪨
beats.comment: Would you have spotted it? 👀 yes / 🪨 no way
beats.bonus: First aid: get out of the water, soak in hot water (about 40-45 °C), get to hospital. An antivenom exists.
beats.caption: Stonefish, the most venomous fish, looks exactly like a rock. What would you do if one stung you? 🧊 ice / 🔥 hot water #stonefish #ocean #animalfacts #venomous Follow Meatball for more 🍝
sources: Australian Museum, Reef Stonefish (Synanceia verrucosa): 'the most venomous fish in the world'; well camouflaged, sits still on the reef; thirteen dorsal spines deliver the toxin; most stings are on feet on reef flats; an antivenom is available — https://australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/reef-stonefish-synanceia-verrucosa-bloch-schneider-1801/
MedlinePlus, Stonefish sting: soak in hot water (40-45 °C) for 30-90 minutes, seek emergency care — https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002854.htm
Queensland Health / Healthdirect: do not apply ice; immerse in hot water as hot as can be tolerated; antivenom available in hospital (checked 2026-10-26)

beats.say: There's one thing that helps a sting. Ice or hot water? Guess.
Subscribe. I face a new animal every day.
See, in reefs from the Red Sea to Australia lives the reef stonefish. The most venomous fish known.
It lies totally still. Lumpy, brown, sometimes covered in algae. It looks exactly like a rock.
Along its back: thirteen spines. Every one carries venom.
Guess one: put ice on it. No. Doctors say no ice.
Guess two: suck the venom out, like in the movies. Also no. Please don't.
Meanwhile, I sat on another rock to think. Same rock. Bad idea.
Wait, here's the thing. The pain is famous. People call it one of the worst pains there is.
The answer: hot water. As hot as you can stand, without burning. Then straight to hospital.
And yes, there's an antivenom. Doctors have had it since the 1950s.
Most stings hit bare feet on reef flats. So wear reef shoes. And watch your step.
I don't have feet. Small win.
Did you guess right? Comment.
Hot water. That's the cure. Hot water is literally where I live.
A baby spider climbed to the tip of a leaf, pointed its butt at the sky, and took off.
beats.headline: SPIDERS CAN FLY
beats.short_title: Yes, It Can Actually Rain Spiders 🕷️ (Meatball vs Spiders #2)
beats.comment: Would you still go outside? 👍 yes / 👎 no
beats.bonus: In 2018, scientists showed spiders balloon on electric fields alone, with no wind at all.
beats.caption: Can spiders fly? Yes, without wings: it's called ballooning. What lifts them? 💨 wind / ⚡ electricity #spiders #ballooning #animalfacts #science Meatball vs Spiders #2. Follow for Part 3 🍝
sources: Morley & Robert 2018, Current Biology 28: 2324-2330, 'Electric fields elicit ballooning in spiders' (spiders sense the atmospheric potential gradient with leg hairs and take off with no airflow) — https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(18)30693-6

Glick 1939, USDA Tech. Bull. 673 (spiders collected by aircraft up to ~15,000 ft) and Darwin, Voyage of the Beagle 1832 (small spiders landed on the ship ~60 miles off the coast) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballooning_(spider) (checked 2026-10-26)
Goulburn, NSW, May 2015: millions of ballooning spiders left fields covered in silk ('angel hair') — https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/millions-baby-spiders-rained-down-australia-180955318/

beats.say: No wings. So what lifts it? Guess.
Subscribe. I face a new animal every day.
See, in 1832, Charles Darwin was sailing sixty miles off South America, and tiny spiders landed on his ship.
Later, planes caught spiders nearly three miles up in the sky.
They let out threads of silk, like little kites. It's called ballooning.
Guess one: they jump really hard. No. They're tiny. That's not it.
Guess two: just the wind. That's what people thought for almost two hundred years. But spiders take off even on calm days.
So I climbed a leaf and tried it myself.
Wait, here's the weird part. In 2018, scientists put spiders in a box with no wind at all.
They switched on an electric field, and the spiders lifted off. The answer is electricity.
The air always carries a faint electric charge. Spiders feel it with tiny hairs on their legs.
In 2015, so many landed in Australia that whole fields turned white with silk.
Did you guess right? Comment.
As for my flight? I'm a meatball. I only go down.
A moray eel shot out of a crack in the reef and snapped up a fish in a flash.
beats.headline: SECOND JAWS
beats.short_title: Moray Eels Have a Second Set of Jaws 🦷
beats.comment: Would you look down its throat? 👍 yes / 👎 no
beats.bonus: Moray eels launch a second set of jaws from the throat to drag prey down (Mehta & Wainwright 2007, Nature).
beats.caption: Moray eels have a second set of jaws hidden in their throat, like the movie Alien. How does it swallow big prey? 💨 suction / 🦷 something else #morayeel #ocean #animalfacts #alien Follow Meatball for more 🍝
sources: Mehta & Wainwright 2007, Nature 449: 79-82, 'Raptorial jaws in the throat help moray eels swallow large prey' (pharyngeal jaws launch forward into the mouth, grab prey and pull it into the throat; morays are poor at suction feeding) — https://doi.org/10.1038/nature06062
National Geographic, 'Moray eels attack with second pair of Alien-style jaws' — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/moray-eels-attack-with-second-pair-of-alien-style-jaws
Moray eels are not venomous; they eat fish, octopus and crustaceans (checked 2026-10-26)

beats.say: But it has a secret weapon. How does it swallow? Guess.
Subscribe. I face a new animal every day.
See, in 2007, two scientists in California filmed morays eating in slow motion.
Morays hide in tiny cracks in the reef, so their heads are long and narrow.
Guess one: it sucks the fish in, like most fish do. No. Morays are bad at suction.
Guess two: venom, to knock the fish out. Also no. Morays aren't venomous.
So I swam over and looked straight down its throat.
Wait. Something in there was looking back at me.
The answer: a second set of jaws, hidden in its throat. They shoot forward, grab the fish, and drag it down.
Scientists said it looks just like the alien in the movie Alien.
It eats fish, crabs and octopus. One bite, then the throat jaws do the rest.
Two sets of jaws. I have zero.
Did you guess right? Comment.
Good news: I'm not on the menu. Mostly because it can't find my throat.
A fly landed on my sandwich, and rubbed its little hands together.
beats.headline: WHAT IT DID NEXT
beats.short_title: House Flies Throw Up on Your Food 🪰
beats.comment: Still eating it after a fly lands? 👍 yes / 👎 no
beats.bonus: House flies can't chew: they spit digestive juices onto solid food and sponge up the soup; they taste with their feet.
beats.caption: Do flies throw up on your food? Yes: house flies spit digestive juice on solid food, then sponge it up. Still eating it? 👍 yes / 👎 no #housefly #gross #animalfacts #insects Follow Meatball for more 🍝
sources: The Conversation / ScienceAlert, 'Do flies really throw up on your food?' (flies have sponging mouthparts and can't chew; they regurgitate digestive juices onto solid food, then suck it up; taste receptors on the feet) — https://www.sciencealert.com/do-flies-really-throw-up-on-your-food-when-they-land-on-it
HowStuffWorks, Housefly Diet (sponging mouthparts) — https://science.howstuffworks.com/environmental/life/zoology/insects-arachnids/housefly3.htm

Junqueira et al. 2017, Scientific Reports 7: 16324 (house flies and blow flies carry hundreds of bacterial species, many on legs and wings; hand-rubbing is grooming) — https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-16353-x

beats.say: What it did next is the gross part. How does it eat? Guess.
Subscribe. I face a new animal every day.
See, in your kitchen, the house fly is the most common fly on Earth. And it lands on everything.
Trash, poop, and then your lunch. It tastes with its feet, so it tastes all of it.
Guess one: it bites off a piece. No. A house fly can't chew. It has no teeth.
Guess two: it just licks it. Closer. But that's not the gross part.
So I let one land on me to watch. Feet first.
Wait. And the hand rubbing? That's not cute. It's cleaning its legs.
The answer: it throws up on your food. It spits digestive juice onto it, the food turns to soup, and it sponges the soup up.
Its mouth works like a sponge on a stick. Solid food has to melt first.
And flies can carry hundreds of kinds of bacteria, on their legs and wings.
Cover your food. Please.
Did you guess right? Comment.
I was the lunch. And it didn't even say thank you.
A hummingbird stopped at a backyard feeder, and a praying mantis grabbed it.
beats.headline: BUG EATS BIRD
beats.loop_say: The food chain is a suggestion. Because
beats.comment: Would you still keep a hummingbird feeder? 👍 yes / 👎 no
beats.bonus: Scientists found 147 cases of mantises catching small birds in 13 countries, most at US hummingbird feeders (Nyffeler et al. 2017).
beats.caption: Can a praying mantis catch a hummingbird? Yes. Scientists found 147 cases. How often? 🦄 freak event / 🐦 more than you think #prayingmantis #hummingbird #animalfacts #birds Follow Meatball for more 🍝
sources: Nyffeler, Maxwell & Remsen 2017, Wilson Journal of Ornithology 129(2): 331-344, 'Bird predation by praying mantises: a global perspective' (147 cases in 13 countries on all continents except Antarctica; >70% in the US, mostly at hummingbird feeders or plants; ruby-throated hummingbird most often; many US cases involve introduced Chinese and European mantises) — https://doi.org/10.1676/16-100.1
Scientific American blog, 'Praying Mantises Catch and Eat Birds Alive' — https://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/artful-amoeba/praying-mantises-catch-and-eat-birds-alive-video/

beats.say: A bug ate a bird. How often does this happen? Guess.
Subscribe. I face a new animal every day.
See, in 2017, three scientists went looking for every report of a mantis catching a bird.
Photos, videos, news stories, birdwatcher notes, from all over the world. They expected a handful.
Guess one: it happened once, a freak accident. No. Not even close.
Guess two: only in some faraway jungle. Also no. Most were right here in the US.
So I hid behind a mantis to stay safe. It turned around and looked at me.
Wait. Here's the thing. The mantis just sits on the feeder and waits.
The answer: they found 147 cases in 13 countries. Most at American hummingbird feeders.
The bird caught most often? The ruby-throated hummingbird.
And many of the mantises were invaders, brought from Asia and Europe.
A bug that eats birds. The food chain is a suggestion.
Did you guess right? Comment.
And if a bug can eat a bird, where does that leave me? Somewhere below the bird.
A man woke up with a red sore on his arm, and the doctor said: brown recluse.
beats.headline: THE BITE THAT ROTS?
beats.short_title: Most Brown Recluse Bites Don't Rot Your Skin 🕷️ (Meatball vs Spiders #3)
beats.comment: Ever blamed a spider for a bite? 👍 yes / 👎 no
beats.bonus: One Kansas home had 2,055 brown recluses in six months and nobody was bitten (Vetter & Barger 2002).
beats.caption: Do brown recluse bites rot your skin? Mostly no: most heal on their own, and many 'recluse bites' are infections. Ever blamed a spider? 👍 yes / 👎 no #brownrecluse #spiders #animalfacts #myths Meatball vs Spiders #3. Follow Meatball for more 🍝
sources: Vetter & Barger 2002, Journal of Medical Entomology 39(6): 948-951, 'An infestation of 2,055 brown recluse spiders and no envenomations in a Kansas home' — https://doi.org/10.1603/0022-2585-39.6.948

Rick Vetter, UC Riverside, 'The Brown Recluse Spider' (most bites are minor and heal without scarring; serious necrosis is uncommon; many 'recluse bites' are misdiagnosed infections such as MRSA, including in areas with no recluses; range is the central and southern US) — https://spiders.ucr.edu/brown-recluse
Wikipedia, Brown recluse spider (checked 2026-10-26) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_recluse_spider

beats.say: But is that true? Do their bites usually rot your skin? Guess.
Subscribe. I face a new animal every day.
See, in 2002, scientists heard about a house in Kansas. A family had lived there for years.
They searched it for six months, and caught two thousand and fifty-five brown recluses.
Guess one: the whole family got bitten. No. Nobody in that house was bitten.
Guess two: recluses live everywhere, so bites are everywhere. Also no. They mostly live in the central and southern US.
So I knocked on one's door to ask. It hid. Very polite.
Wait. Here's the weird part. Doctors diagnose recluse bites in states with no recluses at all.
The answer: most recluse bites are minor and heal on their own. And many 'bites' are really infections, like MRSA.
A bad bite can still need a doctor. It just doesn't happen often.
They're shy. They hide in boxes and shoes, and bite only when pressed against skin.
I'm a meatball. I respect a homebody.
Did you guess right? Comment.
It's called the recluse. It's in the name. It just wants to be left alone.
